endorsements.title: Health Equity Across the AI Lifecycle (HEAAL) framework
endorsements.issuer: Health AI Partnership; PLOS Digital Health (PMID 38723025, doi:10.1371/journal.pdig.0000390)
endorsements.quote: While all standard procedures should be applied to all AI solutions of interest, some procedures are tested at different decision points or follow a different sequential order based on whether the solutions already exist or not.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Examples of patient or community feedback may include representation on AI advisory committees or governance working groups, structured participation through Patient and Family Advisory Councils (PFACs) or community health advisory boards, inclusion in pilot evaluation panels, and community town halls or listening sessions for higher-risk AI solutions.

endorsements.title: Augmenting research consent: should large language models (LLMs) be used for informed consent to clinical research?
endorsements.quote: Public engagement forums and mechanisms for participant feedback are essential to ensure trust in these systems, alongside stringent adherence to data privacy and security standards.

endorsements.title: Responsible AI in mental healthcare: policy directions and stakeholder insights
endorsements.quote: Similarly, individuals subject to monitoring or triage should be informed of their rights, options, and the nature of algorithmic decision-making.

evidence.title: Increasing Use of a Postpartum and Newborn Chatbot among Birthing Individuals and Caregivers: Development and Implementation Study
evidence.outcome: Chatbot reach after adding chatbot information to discharge paperwork
evidence.effect: Postpartum reach changed from 63.6% to 63.9% (OR 1.02, 95% CI 0.90-1.15); newborn reach changed from 66.2% to 64.6% (OR 0.93, 95% CI 0.83-1.05). Neither change was significant.
evidence.quote: No significant changes in reach were found after launching the updated version of the newborn and postpartum outreach and chatbot content, nor after including the chatbot information in patients’ discharge paperwork ( Table 5 ); thus, we focused on results in the combined analyses for the full time period.
evidence.sample_unit: chatbot recipients (6505 birthing individuals and 7489 newborn caregivers)

commentary.bottom_line: One real-deployment study tested a single form of proactive communication, adding chatbot information to discharge paperwork, and found no significant change in chatbot reach among postpartum patients or newborn caregivers. Two frameworks and two commentaries endorse proactive communication and community feedback, but no study has measured whether this practice improves awareness or trust among disadvantaged groups.

perspectives.view: The only test is a descriptive before-and-after comparison. Postpartum reach moved from 63.6% to 63.9% (OR 1.02, 95% CI 0.90-1.15), and newborn reach moved from 66.2% to 64.6% (OR 0.93, 95% CI 0.83-1.05). The observational design and the indirect outcome, chatbot reach rather than patient awareness of AI use, support very low certainty.

In this deployment, adding information to discharge paperwork did not significantly change how many patients the chatbot reached. The finding suggests that written notice alone may not be enough. The study did not test other channels such as town halls, advisory councils, or clinician conversations, so their effect is unknown.

The study population included patients with limited English proficiency and had a racial and ethnic minority focus. The null result in this population suggests that paperwork-based notice may not close awareness gaps. The study did not report results for Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy patients.

Among nearly 14,000 chatbot recipients, roughly one in three was not reached by the tool either before or after the paperwork change. Patients who miss written notices may not learn that an AI tool is part of their care. This study offers no evidence on whether patients knew how to reach a human instead.

commentary.research_gap: No study measured whether proactive communication increases patient or community awareness of AI use, understanding of privacy-practice changes, or use of feedback channels. Comparative studies of communication methods, such as advisory councils, community forums, multilingual outreach, and clinician-delivered notice, should use awareness and trust as outcomes and should report results for disadvantaged subgroups.
commentary.underserved_note: The single test included limited English proficiency and racial and ethnic minority populations and found no significant change in reach after written notice was added. It did not report Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy subgroups, so the evidence cannot show whether any communication approach reaches those groups.
